summary: ECH keys must be configured into TLS servers, which may use different TLS libraries. This document specifies a PEM file format for them, like RFC 7468.

plainLanguage.summary: Encrypted ClientHello requires TLS servers to load ECH keys and configuration. This RFC defines a PEM file layout that different server software can use, while requiring the private key to stay out of DNS.

questions: what is an ech pem file
what is the ech pem file format
subtitle: A PEM file format for configuring Encrypted ClientHello keys on TLS servers.

tldr.problem: TLS servers need ECH key pairs, but different TLS libraries benefit from a common file format for those keys and configurations.
tldr.mechanism: A PEM ECH file contains zero or one PKCS #8 private key followed by one encoded ECHConfigList using the ECHCONFIG label.
tldr.outcome: The format supports sharing ECH configuration across servers; the private key MUST NOT be published in DNS.

today: RFC 9934 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Shared ECH File Format
sections.content:
Encrypted ClientHello (ECH) provides confidentiality for server names and other ClientHello content in TLS. An ECHConfigList is published in an HTTPS or SVCB DNS record and contains one or more ECHConfig values.

TLS servers need the associated key pairs, and can be built with different TLS libraries. RFC 9934 defines a common PEM format for their ECH keys and configurations.
sections.plainLanguage: ECH requires TLS servers to load key material and a public configuration. A shared PEM layout lets different server software read those values in a consistent form.

sections.title: The ECHConfig PEM File
sections.content:
A PEM ECH file contains zero or one private key and one encoded ECHConfigList. If present, the private key comes first and MUST be a PEM-encoded PKCS #8 PrivateKey. The ECHConfigList follows as the public part, using the PEM delimiter label ECHCONFIG.

The public part is the base64-encoded form of an ECHConfigList that can be published in DNS. If a private key is present, the list MUST include a matching ECHConfig. Content after the list SHOULD be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The file puts the private key first, if one is included, and the public configuration after it. The public configuration must contain a key that matches the private key.

sections.title: Configuration Lists
sections.content:
An ECHConfigList may contain several ECHConfig values, for example with different extensions or public_name values. The values appear in decreasing order of preference.

A TLS server might use several files in its overall configuration, such as using only some ECHConfigList values for retry_configs in an ECH fallback scenario.
sections.plainLanguage: A configuration list can contain several public configurations, ordered from more preferred to less preferred. A server may select configuration lists from multiple files.

sections.title: Protecting the Private Key
sections.content:
Anyone with read access to the file system can access cryptographic keys stored there. The RFC says to use the same protections used for a server's PEM-encoded HTTPS certificate private key.

Only the ECHConfigList is published in DNS. The private key in an ECH PEM file MUST NOT be published there. The document has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Protect the file as carefully as a TLS certificate private key. Publish the ECHConfigList, never the private key, in DNS.
